hints: Consider what happens to several diameter readings when the same measuring fault affects every reading, compared with when the effect varies from reading to reading.
One error gives a consistent offset from the true diameter; the other makes repeated readings spread on either side of the true value.
walkthrough: A systematic error introduces the same bias each time the micrometer reading is taken, so all measured diameters are consistently too large or consistently too small by a fixed amount.
A random error varies unpredictably between readings, so repeated diameter measurements scatter about the true value rather than all moving together in one direction.
The two effects differ because a systematic bias does not average out through repetition, whereas random scatter can be reduced by taking and averaging repeated readings.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that a systematic error makes each measured diameter consistently higher or lower than the true diameter by a fixed amount.
Explains that a random error makes repeated diameter readings scatter about the true diameter.

hints: Separate how finely the micrometer can resolve the wire diameter from how close its measured diameter is to the true value.
For this micrometer, precision can be described by its 0.01 mm smallest division; accuracy concerns closeness to the true diameter.
walkthrough: Precision here is the resolution of the measuring instrument: the smallest division of the micrometer is 0.01 mm, so it can distinguish diameter changes at that scale.
Accuracy is how close the measured diameter is to the true diameter of the wire.
Thus a micrometer may give readings to 0.01 mm without necessarily being accurate if, for example, a zero error shifts every reading away from the true diameter.

ai_rubric.observable: States that precision is set by the micrometer's smallest division or gives its 0.01 mm resolution.
States that accuracy is the closeness of the measured diameter to the true diameter.
